questions.problem: Change the order of integration in the double integral ${\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2-{y}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14154008/assets/48a1ef0d61b8b81e2fa0649b95a329099d48a802a5339d730f2da9cf8b59f547.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It is a type II region, and its type II representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,1\le x\le 2-{y}^{2}\}.
$$

Notice that the top boundary of the region, written in the form $x=x(y),$ is

$$
x=2-{y}^{2}\,⟹\,y=\sqrt{2-x},
$$

and the bottom boundary of the region is

$$
y=0.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type I region. The type I representation of the region is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{2-x}\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14154008/assets/22d41ecc443e1520035f52fefe524d88062432ab1643aa19b2e0b76185b191a0.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2-{y}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2-x}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Change the order of integration in the double integral 
${\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{y}^{2}-1}^{1-y}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14154008/assets/e6b8889f9e8025cfca1ee0ae61b67a2f7ec9ec4aee15fab78d2f418a655bbcb8.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. This is a type II region, and its type II representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,{y}^{2}-1\le x\le 1-y\}.
$$

To change the order of integration, we need to split $D$ into two type I regions.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14154008/assets/52640b30ded8bf2cd19fe7860c7640bde3c8427ae8978f32fb8020b2f7215468.png)

Notice that the bottom and top boundaries of the left region, written in the form $y=y(x),$  are 

$\,$ $y=0\,$ and $\,y=\sqrt{x+1}.$

Also, the bottom and top boundaries of the right region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ are

$\,$ $y=0\,$ and $\,y=1-x.$ 

So, we can write $D$ as a union of

$$
{D}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 0,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{x+1}\}
$$

and

$$
{D}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1-x\}.
$$

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{y}^{2}-1}^{1-y}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x+1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-x}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14154008/assets/a85f82756c621bf88b95451f54343be863345278f361fd0f0dd82f5d01c0cb5b.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. This is a type I region, and its type I representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,{x}^{3}\le y\le 1\}.
$$

Notice that the left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
x=0,
$$

and the right boundary is

$$
y={x}^{3}\,⟹\,x=\sqrt[3]{y}.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type II region. Its type II representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,0\le x\le \sqrt[3]{y}\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14154008/assets/8243a8c60e4b8b4846d330a00a090d6f93f94f17323c1d0a88d486ba77745451.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{3}}^{1}\frac{3{x}^{5}}{\sqrt{{x}^{6}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{y}}\frac{3{x}^{5}}{\sqrt{{x}^{6}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{y}}\frac{3{x}^{5}}{\sqrt{{x}^{6}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3{[\frac{2}{6}\sqrt{{x}^{6}+{y}^{2}}]}_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\sqrt{2{y}^{2}}-\sqrt{{y}^{2}})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y(\sqrt{2}-1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{(\sqrt{2}-1)}{2}[{y}^{2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}-1}{2}(1-0) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}-1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Change the order of integration and evaluate the double integral 
${\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{4-{x}^{2}}4x{e}^{8y-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14154008/assets/262e1b0c4e0ddf338c527b487fcadc85baac12712f91cb4c54b771e49add25b9.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It is a type I region, and its type I representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 4-{x}^{2}\}.
$$

Notice that the left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
x=0,
$$

and the right boundary of the region is

$$
y=4-{x}^{2}\,⟹\,x=\sqrt{4-y}.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type II region. The type II representation of the region is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 4,\,0\le x\le \sqrt{4-y}\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14154008/assets/48c874b069b55599f76a8fe1aa50c5f4db36ff8943d264a107452668d689174b.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{4-{x}^{2}}4x{e}^{8y-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-y}}4x{e}^{8y-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{e}^{8y-{y}^{2}}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-y}}4x\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{e}^{8y-{y}^{2}}\cdot 2{x}^{2}\,{|}_{0}^{\sqrt{4-y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}2(4-y){e}^{8y-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={e}^{8y-{y}^{2}}\,{|}_{0}^{4} \\  & ={e}^{8(4)-{4}^{2}}-{e}^{8(0)-{0}^{2}} \\  & ={e}^{16}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Change the order of integration in the double integral 
$\displaystyle \int_0^1 \int_{y^3}^{1} f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}x \: \textrm{d}y.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14154008/assets/47b8a129674d4644593741607e0efd5dea1ffde45357f327e3af4e08d0bf423d.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It is a type II region, and its type II representation is

$$
D= \big\{ (x,y) \::\: 0 \leq y \leq1, \quad y^3 \leq x \leq 1 \big\},
$$

Notice that the top boundary of the region, written in the form $x=x(y),$ is

$$
x = y^3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y = \sqrt[3]{x},
$$

and the bottom boundary of the region is

$$
y = 0.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type I region. The type I representation of the region is

$$
D= \big\{ (x,y) \::\: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \quad 0 \leq y \leq \sqrt[3]{x} \big\}.
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14154008/assets/e627a8750d3f5055b3936d47100fc51ae68926dfdc0c53d020638c9ef99f9b27.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{1}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{x}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Swapping the Order of Integration on a Partitioned Region
canonical_examples.problem: Change the order of integration in the double integral $\displaystyle \int_0^1\int_{2x}^{3-x} f(x,y)\,\textrm{d}y\,\textrm{d}x .$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14154008/assets/47f6b583b2dd059ad8df49b0ca4374a964b4a28e91eb242a0dd3c7b8476fd26e.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. This is a type I region, and its type I representation is

$$
D=\big\{ (x,y) \::\: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \quad 2x \leq y \leq 3-x \big\}.
$$

To change the order of integration, we need to split $D$ into two type II regions. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14154008/assets/35b4b57f26c7903189899ec284faa39bb70fb3a80397b772376358d4d86b3ec1.png)

Notice that the right boundary of the lower region, written in the form $x=x(y),$  is 

$$
x=\dfrac{y}{2}.
$$

Also, the right boundary of the upper region, written in the form $x=x(y),$ is

$$
x=3-y.
$$

So, we can write $D$ as a union of

$$
D_1 = \Big\{ (x,y) \::\: 0 \leq y \leq 2, \quad 0 \leq x \leq \dfrac{y}{2} \Big\}
$$

and

$$
D_2 = \Big\{ (x,y) \::\: 2 \leq y \leq 3, \quad 0 \leq x \leq 3-y \Big\}.
$$

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2x}^{3-x}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{y/2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{2}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3-y}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Evaluating a Double Integral by Swapping the Order of Integration
canonical_examples.problem: Change the order of integration and evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle{\int_0^{1} \int_{\sqrt{x}}^{1 } 9\sqrt{y^3+1}\,\textrm{d}y\,\textrm{d}x}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14154008/assets/1045aaad8025b20309b92477b4a1cf98e138064210c6fbc960c64ec26c9951df.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. This is a type I region, and its type I representation is

$$
D = \big\{ (x,y) \::\: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \quad \sqrt{x} \leq y \leq 1 \big\}.
$$

Notice that the left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
x=0,
$$

and the right boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
y = \sqrt{x} 
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
x=y^2.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as type II region. Its type II representation is

$$
D = \big\{ (x,y) \::\: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \quad 0 \leq x \leq y^2 \big\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14154008/assets/40cbaaff270daddf4b60115cc272fbc8b165b83b8823d19de2c19802617ebdb4.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\sqrt{x}}^{1}9\sqrt{{y}^{3}+1}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}9\sqrt{{y}^{3}+1}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{y}^{3}+1}[{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}y \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{y}^{3}+1}[x\,]_{0}^{{y}^{2}}\,dy \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{1}3{y}^{2}({y}^{3}+1)^{1/2}\,dy \\  & =3{[\frac{2}{3}({y}^{3}+1)^{3/2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[2({y}^{3}+1)^{3/2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =2(2)^{3/2}-2 \\  & =4\sqrt{2}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we want to evaluate the repeated integral

$$
\int_{\color{black}0}^{\color{black}2} \int_{\color{black}x/2}^{\color{black}1} \, e^{y^2}\,\textrm{d}{\color{black}y} \, \textrm{d}{\color{black}x}.
$$

The expression "$\,\textrm{d}y\,\textrm{d}x\,$" tells us that we should integrate first with respect to $y.$ This is problematic, though, as the integrand $e^{y^2}$ does not have an elementary antiderivative. So, what can we do?

In cases like this, **reversing the order of integration** from $\, \textrm{d}y\,\textrm{d}x\,$ to $\, \textrm{d}x\,\textrm{d}y$ might help. But beware! Because the domain of integration is non-rectangular, we can't just swap the order of the integrals. This is because, to integrate with respect to $x,$ we can't have $x$'s in the limits. So we need to work out new limits.

When swapping the order of integration, it is helpful to sketch the region $D$ over which we're integrating.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14154008/assets/d3ee76083ae3917b4585fce7227475d3e0471550f193f2fa437be3ebf92dc288.png)

To integrate first with respect to $y,$ we imagine a line parallel to the $y$-axis, as shown above. Note the following:

- This line *enters* the region through the curve $\color{black} y=\dfrac{x}{2}$ and *leaves* at $\color{black} y=1.$ These are the variable limits for $y.$

- The minimum value of $x$ is $\color{black}0,$ and the maximum value of $x$ is ${\color{black}2}.$

So, the integral we were initially given is over the following type I region:

$$
D=\left \{  (x,y) \: : \: {\color{black}0} \leq x \leq {\color{black}2}, \quad {\color{black}\dfrac{x}{2}} \leq y \leq {\color{black}1} \right\}
$$

However, since we now want to integrate first with respect to $x,$ we need the limits for $x$ to be functions of $y$, and we need the limits of $y$ to be constants. To work these out, we redraw the region, but this time we imagine a line parallel to the $x$-axis.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14154008/assets/c80ae995a92aba4f535b5e5a01305f8ffbf790ad1f97ee8db4f368e4bfabb0c1.png)

- The line *enters* the region at $\color{black}x=0$ and *leaves* the region at $\color{black} x=2y.$ So these are our variable limits for $x.$

- The minimum value of $\color{black}y$ is $\color{black}0,$ and the maximum value of $y$ is ${\color{black}1}.$

So, we can consider $D$ to be the following type II region:

$$
D=\left \{  (x,y):\quad {\color{black}0} \leq x \leq {\color{black}2y}, \quad {\color{black}0} \leq y \leq {\color{black}1} \right\}
$$

Now that we have expressed the region $D$ as a type II region, we're ready to swap the order of integration and finally calculate our integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{x/2}^{1}\,{e}^{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2y}{e}^{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{{y}^{2}}[{\int }_{0}^{2y}\text{d}x]\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{{y}^{2}}[x]_{0}^{2y}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2y{e}^{{y}^{2}}dy \\  & ={[{e}^{{y}^{2}}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =e-1.\end{aligned}
$$
